Where it began

Ian Bell was born in Coventry on 11 April 1982. His family came from Dunchurch, near Rugby, and he learned the game at the village club there before going to Princethorpe College, where he was already in the first eleven in year 7.

He was spotted early. On an England Under-19 tour of New Zealand he made 91 and 115, and he went on to captain the Under-19 side. In 2001, at 19 years and 56 days, he became Warwickshire's youngest centurion, and that September they made him their youngest capped player.

The player

He arrived in Test cricket at The Oval in 2004 and made 70 in his first innings. Over the next eleven years he played 118 Tests, scoring 7,727 runs at 42.69 with 22 hundreds and 46 fifties. His best was 235 against India in 2011, the summer England climbed to the top of the world rankings. He held 99 catches, many of them crouching close to the bat.

He was there for the Ashes wins of 2005 and 2009, for the 3–1 victory in Australia in 2010–11, and for 2013, when hundreds at Trent Bridge and Lord's helped make him man of the series. In 2006 he made a century in three Tests running against Pakistan, the first Englishman to do so since Graham Gooch.

What made him special

Elegance, mostly. He timed the ball rather than hit it, and his cover drive was the shot people came to see. He could bat anywhere from opener to number six, and he was a sharp fielder close in, with reflexes to match.

If there was one thing he wished he had done better, it was turning lovely forties into big hundreds in his early years. Later, the hundreds came in a rush. And once, against South Africa in 2008, he was out for 199, the first Englishman to fall one short of a double. He made amends three years later with 235.

Away from the middle

He was made an MBE after the 2005 Ashes, named the ICC's Emerging Player of the Year in 2006 and chosen as a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. He scored more than 20,000 first-class runs, retired in 2020, and went into coaching, working with England Under-19s, Derbyshire, New Zealand and, in 2024, as Sri Lanka's batting coach.

And finally

As a boy he went to Coventry City's football school of excellence while supporting their great rivals, Aston Villa. He has been a regular at Villa Park ever since, which shows the same loyalty he gave Warwickshire for his whole county career.
